newsitem.title: USA: N. Korea said set to meet MIA families on Friday.
newsitem.headline: N. Korea said set to meet MIA families on Friday.

text.p: In a sign of quickening cooperation on a crucial bilateral issue, North Korea has agreed to meet on Friday with the families of American soldiers missing from the Korean War, the United States said on Monday.

It will be the first meeting between North Korea and the American families "and we view this as a positive sign of North Korea's interest in making progress on this humanitarian issue," John Dinger, a State Department spokesman, told reporters.
"From the U.S. perspective, the meeting (on the missing-in-action or MIA issue) is moving in a productive direction," he said.

However, a military official at the Pentagon, who asked not to be identified, said he understood that so far only one member of one family had agreed to attend the meeting. There are about 8,100 American troops counted as still missing from the 1950-53 Korean War.
U.S. officials said the MIA discussions, which began on Sunday, were taking place at an undisclosed location in New York City and were expected to last through at least Thursday.
"The first round wound up on Sunday night with an agreement to continue," said Air Force Lt. Col. Joan Ferguson, a Pentagon spokeswoman.

U.S.-North Korean talks on the 8,100 missing troops were last held in May 1996. They led to an agreement that resulted in joint recovery of the remains of a American Army corporal, but were derailed when a North Korean submarine loaded with commandos ran aground last September off South Korea.

The United States paid North Korea $2 million to cover the cost of last year's search operation, but has asked Pyongyang to stop returning remains of suspected U.S. troops until further joint searches can be set up in order to make identifications easier.

The Pentagon announced last week that the new round of talks would also deal with U.S. questions about reports of Americans possibly living in North Korea. Washington also wants access to North Korean files on Americans held prisoner in the North during the war.

U.S. officials said the third topic of the negotiations includes a possible schedule for resuming joint excavations at sites believed to contain remains of U.S. servicemen buried or shot down during the war.
Friday's meeting with the MIA families -- also scheduled for New York -- will not be open to the public to protect the families' privacy, Dinger said.

The latest MIA talks are separate from negotiations that broke off last month in New York in which the United States and South Korea urged Pyongyang to begin four-way peace talks with China to negotiate a formal end to the 1950-53 Korean War.

However, the MIA talks are related in a broad sense to U.S. efforts to defuse tensions on the Korean peninsula, where North Korea's million-man army confronts 37,000 U.S. soldiers and the South Korean army across the heavily-fortified demilitarized zone.

The United States has said its willingness to give the Stalinist regime in North Korea formal diplomatic recognition and lift trade sanctions against it depends on Pyongyang's willingness to demilitarize the peninsula, resolve the remaining MIA cases and meet U.S. concerns about North Korean missile sales. U.S.-North Korea talks on missile sales are set for next week in New York.
